questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four basic elements of a State?
options: A defined territory
A permanent population
Sovereignty
A written constitution
questions.explanation: The four essential elements of a State are population, territory, government and sovereignty; a written constitution is common but not a defining requirement (e.g. Britain has no single written constitution).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Government, as a political concept, is best understood as the
options: machinery or set of institutions through which the will of the State is formulated and enforced
total land area and natural resources of a country
collection of private businesses operating in a country
sum of all citizens residing in a State
questions.explanation: Government refers to the institutions and processes (legislature, executive, judiciary) through which a State exercises its authority and administers public affairs.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The concept of the 'Social Contract' as propounded by political philosophers holds that
options: individuals surrender some natural freedoms to a sovereign authority in exchange for order and protection
citizens owe no obligations to the State whatsoever
the State has no legitimate authority over its citizens
government must always be hereditary
questions.explanation: Social contract theorists such as Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau argued that legitimate government arises from an implicit agreement in which people give up some liberties for security and civil order.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which political philosopher is most associated with the view that life in the state of nature was 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'?
options: Karl Marx
John Locke
Thomas Hobbes
Jean-Jacques Rousseau
questions.explanation: Thomas Hobbes, in his work 'Leviathan', described the pre-political state of nature in these terms to justify the need for an all-powerful sovereign.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: John Locke's theory of the social contract differed from Hobbes' mainly in that Locke
options: rejected the idea of natural rights entirely
argued that only a monarchy could ever be legitimate
believed the sovereign's power should be absolute and unchallengeable
believed government exists to protect natural rights, and could be legitimately overthrown if it failed to do so
questions.explanation: Locke held that government is a trustee of the people's natural rights (life, liberty, property), and that citizens retain the right to resist a government that betrays this trust.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Pressure groups differ from political parties mainly in that pressure groups
options: seek to influence government policy without contesting elections to gain power
are funded exclusively by government subvention
are formally recognised organs of government
always seek to win political power by contesting elections
questions.explanation: Pressure groups (interest groups) aim to influence government decisions on specific issues but, unlike political parties, do not put up candidates to contest for governmental power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The term 'public opinion' in government refers to
options: the official position of the ruling political party alone
the collective views held by a significant section of the citizenry on a public issue
the personal opinion of the head of state
a decision reached exclusively by the judiciary
questions.explanation: Public opinion represents the aggregate attitudes and views of citizens on matters of public concern, and it can influence government policy in a democracy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes a 'de jure' government from a 'de facto' government?
options: There is no meaningful distinction between the two terms
A de jure government has no constitution, while a de facto government always has one
A de jure government is legally constituted, while a de facto government is one actually in control regardless of legal title
A de facto government is always elected, while a de jure government is always military
questions.explanation: 'De jure' means 'by right' or 'in law', describing a government with lawful title to rule, while 'de facto' means 'in fact', describing a government that actually exercises power, such as after a coup.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The rule of law, as a principle of good government, essentially means that
options: laws only apply to ordinary citizens and not to public officials
no one, including government officials, is above the law, and all are subject to the ordinary law of the land
the government may act however it wishes provided it does not lose elections
military decrees automatically override the constitution
questions.explanation: The rule of law requires equality before the law, supremacy of the law over arbitrary power, and that even government officials are accountable to the law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A theocracy is a system of government in which
options: power is divided equally among several independent states
power rests entirely with elected civilian representatives
political authority is believed to be derived from and exercised in accordance with religious law
the military rules directly without any religious basis
questions.explanation: In a theocracy, governance is conducted according to religious principles, with religious leaders or divine law regarded as the ultimate source of political authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A plebiscite is best described as
options: an appointment made by the head of state without any vote
a direct vote by the electorate on a specific important political question
a court ruling on a constitutional matter
a routine election of members of the legislature
questions.explanation: A plebiscite (or referendum) is a form of direct democracy in which citizens vote directly on a particular issue, such as a constitutional change or self-determination.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a key advantage of a unitary system of government?
options: It automatically prevents ethnic or regional tension
It eliminates the possibility of any central authority
It promotes uniformity of policy and avoids the duplication of governmental functions across regions
It always guarantees greater regional autonomy than a federal system
questions.explanation: Because power is centralised, a unitary system can ensure uniform laws and policies nationwide and avoid the overlap of functions that can occur between central and regional governments.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major reason often given for Nigeria's adoption of federalism is that it
options: removes the need for a written constitution
accommodates the country's ethnic, religious and cultural diversity by allowing regional self-government
abolishes the need for a central government entirely
guarantees that a single ethnic group will always control the central government
questions.explanation: Federalism was adopted in Nigeria partly to manage its considerable ethnic, religious and cultural diversity by granting constituent units a measure of self-governance.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In a true federation, which of the following is an essential feature?
options: The absence of any judiciary to settle disputes between tiers of government
The complete absence of a central government
The subordination of state governments entirely to the will of the central government
A written constitution that clearly divides powers between the central and regional governments
questions.explanation: A genuine federation requires a written and usually rigid constitution that constitutionally allocates specific powers to the central and regional/state governments, with an independent judiciary to arbitrate disputes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The exclusive legislative list in Nigeria's constitution contains matters
options: on which both federal and state legislatures may make laws concurrently
on which only the National Assembly (federal legislature) may make laws
on which only state Houses of Assembly may make laws
that are reserved exclusively for local government councils
questions.explanation: Under Nigeria's federal constitution, the exclusive legislative list covers matters such as defence and foreign affairs, on which only the National Assembly has power to legislate.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a matter typically found on the concurrent legislative list in a federation?
options: Defence of the federation
Currency and coinage
Declaration of war
Health and education
questions.explanation: Concurrent list matters, such as health and education, are those on which both federal and state legislatures may legislate, though federal law usually prevails in case of conflict.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key distinguishing feature of a parliamentary system, as practised in Britain, is that
options: there is a strict separation between the executive and legislative branches
the Prime Minister and Cabinet remain in office only as long as they retain the confidence (support) of Parliament
the judiciary has the power to remove the Prime Minister at will
the head of government is directly elected by the entire population separately from the legislature
questions.explanation: In parliamentary systems, the executive is fused with and drawn from the legislature, and the government can be forced to resign through a vote of no confidence.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One major disadvantage often associated with the presidential system of government is that it
options: guarantees that laws are made without any legislative input
makes it impossible for the legislature to check the executive at all
can lead to deadlock between the executive and legislature when they are controlled by rival parties
eliminates the principle of separation of powers entirely
questions.explanation: Because the executive and legislature are separately elected and can be controlled by different parties, a presidential system can experience gridlock, particularly over budgets and legislation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The power of 'judicial review' refers to the ability of the courts to
options: examine and, where necessary, declare an act of the executive or legislature unconstitutional and void
draft and pass new legislation directly
appoint members of the executive cabinet
dissolve the legislature at will
questions.explanation: Judicial review empowers courts to assess whether laws or executive actions conform to the constitution, striking down those that do not, thereby acting as a check on the other arms of government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the Nigerian federal system, the National Assembly is made up of
options: the Senate and the House of Representatives
the House of Representatives and the State Houses of Assembly
the Federal Executive Council and the Senate
the Senate only
questions.explanation: Nigeria operates a bicameral National Assembly consisting of the Senate (upper chamber) and the House of Representatives (lower chamber).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under Nigeria's 1999 Constitution (as amended), the President is elected for a term of
options: four years, with no limit on the number of terms
four years, renewable once
six years, non-renewable
five years, renewable once
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution provides for a four-year presidential term, with an individual eligible for re-election to serve a maximum of two terms.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principal function of the Public Accounts Committee in the legislature is to
options: draft the annual national budget for the executive
appoint judges to the Supreme Court
scrutinise how public funds appropriated by the legislature have been spent by the executive
conduct foreign diplomatic negotiations
questions.explanation: The Public Accounts Committee examines the audited accounts of government ministries and agencies to ensure appropriated funds were properly and lawfully spent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a constitutional check that the legislature holds over the executive in a presidential system?
options: The power to declare war without any executive involvement
The power to impeach the President for gross misconduct
The power to dissolve the judiciary
The power to appoint all federal judges without any confirmation process
questions.explanation: As part of the checks and balances system, the legislature can remove a sitting President through the constitutionally prescribed impeachment process for gross misconduct.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The independence of the judiciary is best safeguarded by
options: placing the judiciary directly under the control of the legislature
allowing the executive sole discretion to remove any judge at any time
security of tenure for judges and the constitutional insulation of judicial appointments and removal from political interference
requiring judges to be re-elected annually by popular vote
questions.explanation: Judicial independence is protected mainly through security of tenure, fixed remuneration, and constitutionally regulated appointment/removal procedures that shield judges from undue political pressure.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A 'Bill' becomes an 'Act' of the National Assembly in Nigeria when it
options: is merely debated at its second reading
is first introduced on the floor of the Senate
has been passed by both chambers of the National Assembly and assented to by the President
is referred to a committee for further review
questions.explanation: A Bill must pass through both the Senate and the House of Representatives and receive Presidential assent (or be passed over a Presidential veto) before it becomes law as an Act.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which arm of government is primarily responsible for the day-to-day administration of ministries and government agencies?
options: The Legislature
The Judiciary
The Electoral Commission
The Executive
questions.explanation: The executive arm, through the President/Governor and appointed ministers/commissioners, superintends the ministries, departments and agencies that carry out government policy daily.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Federal Executive Council in Nigeria is composed mainly of
options: Supreme Court Justices exclusively
only members of the National Assembly
the President, the Vice President, and Ministers
State Governors and their deputies
questions.explanation: The Federal Executive Council is the highest executive decision-making body, chaired by the President and comprising the Vice President and federal Ministers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Citizenship by registration, under Nigerian law, is generally available to
options: any foreigner who has merely visited Nigeria on a tourist visa
a company incorporated in Nigeria
a woman who is or has been married to a citizen of Nigeria, upon application
a person born outside Nigeria to two non-Nigerian parents
questions.explanation: Under the 1999 Constitution, a woman married to a Nigerian citizen may apply to be registered as a Nigerian citizen, subject to prescribed conditions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Citizenship by naturalisation in Nigeria is generally granted to a foreigner who
options: has resided continuously in Nigeria for a prescribed period and satisfies other statutory conditions, then applies and is granted a certificate
is simply born on Nigerian soil
marries a Nigerian citizen and needs no further formal process
is the child of a Nigerian citizen born abroad
questions.explanation: Naturalisation requires a qualifying period of lawful residence in Nigeria and good character, after which the President may grant a certificate of naturalisation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following rights is classified as a 'fundamental human right' under Chapter IV of Nigeria's 1999 Constitution?
options: The right to personal liberty
The right to freely available healthcare
The right to a minimum wage
The right to free primary education
questions.explanation: Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution guarantees justiciable fundamental rights such as the right to life, personal liberty, fair hearing and freedom of expression; the others fall under non-justiciable Fundamental Objectives (Chapter II).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy in Nigeria's Constitution are generally regarded as
options: fully enforceable in a court of law like fundamental rights
irrelevant to government policy formulation
applicable only to state governments and not the federal government
non-justiciable, meaning courts cannot compel government to implement them directly
questions.explanation: Chapter II of the Constitution sets out socio-economic goals for the State to pursue, but section 6(6)(c) makes these objectives non-justiciable, so they cannot ordinarily be enforced by the courts.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The right to fair hearing includes the principle that
options: a court may convict without hearing the defence
a person should not be a judge in his own cause (nemo judex in causa sua)
trials may proceed without informing the accused of the charge
an accused person has no right to legal representation
questions.explanation: One of the twin pillars of natural justice underlying fair hearing is nemo judex in causa sua — that no one should adjudicate a matter in which they have a personal interest.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A writ of habeas corpus is a legal remedy used mainly to
options: dissolve an unlawfully constituted political party
challenge the lawfulness of a person's detention and secure their release if the detention is unlawful
compel the government to build more prisons
appoint a new head of the judiciary
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus is a court order requiring that a detained person be brought before a court so the legality of their detention can be examined.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Civic responsibilities of a citizen typically include
options: obeying the law and paying taxes promptly
the right to own property exclusively
the right to free movement only
the right to vote only, with no accompanying obligations
questions.explanation: Citizenship confers both rights and duties; obeying the law and paying taxes are core civic responsibilities expected of every citizen in return for the protection and services the State provides.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best defines a 'stateless person'?
options: A person who has dual citizenship of two countries
A person who is not recognised as a citizen or national by any State under its laws
A person who owns no landed property
A person who has renounced voting rights
questions.explanation: Statelessness occurs when no country recognises a person as its citizen, leaving them without the legal protections and rights that citizenship confers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A political party is best defined as an organised group that
options: is formed purely for religious worship
is a permanent branch of the civil service
exists solely to lobby government without contesting elections
seeks to win governmental power by presenting candidates for election and implementing a common programme
questions.explanation: Political parties are distinguished from pressure groups by their goal of winning control of government through elections, based on a shared ideology or programme.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A one-party system of government is often criticised mainly because it
options: guarantees free and fair elections
limits political competition and can suppress opposing viewpoints
eliminates the possibility of corruption
always produces the most efficient economic policies
questions.explanation: Where only one party is legally permitted, genuine political competition and choice for the electorate are curtailed, and dissenting views may be suppressed.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is an advantage commonly claimed for a two-party system?
options: It guarantees representation for every minority interest in society
It removes the need for elections altogether
It tends to produce clear, stable parliamentary majorities and simplifies voter choice
It always eliminates political conflict entirely
questions.explanation: A two-party system, as in the United States, tends to produce decisive electoral outcomes and a straightforward choice for voters, though it may limit representation of minority viewpoints.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The electoral system in which a country is divided into constituencies and the candidate with the highest number of votes wins is known as
options: Proportional Representation
First-Past-The-Post (simple plurality)
The Single Transferable Vote
Indirect election
questions.explanation: Under First-Past-The-Post, the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins outright, even without an absolute majority, unlike proportional representation systems.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Proportional representation as an electoral system is designed mainly to
options: ensure that only the ruling party's candidates can be elected
guarantee that only two parties can ever win seats
allocate legislative seats to parties in close proportion to the share of votes each party receives
eliminate political parties from the electoral process
questions.explanation: Proportional representation seeks to match a party's share of parliamentary seats closely with its share of the total votes cast, giving smaller parties fairer representation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Universal adult suffrage means that
options: every adult citizen who meets the basic age requirement has the right to vote, regardless of gender, income or education
only male citizens are permitted to vote
only property owners are permitted to vote
only literate citizens are permitted to vote
questions.explanation: Universal adult suffrage removes restrictions such as property ownership, literacy, gender or income as conditions for voting, granting the franchise to all qualifying adult citizens.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In Nigeria, the body constitutionally responsible for organising, conducting and supervising elections into federal and state legislative and executive offices is the
options: National Assembly
Federal Judicial Service Commission
Code of Conduct Bureau
Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC)
questions.explanation: INEC is the constitutionally established body charged with organising elections into the offices of President, Governors, and members of the National and State Assemblies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Political apathy refers to
options: the formation of a new political party
a lack of interest or willingness to participate in political activities such as voting
strong loyalty to a particular political party
active and enthusiastic participation in politics
questions.explanation: Political apathy describes indifference or disengagement from political processes, often reflected in low voter turnout or lack of interest in public affairs.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Political socialisation refers to the process by which
options: a government dissolves a legislature before its term ends
individuals acquire their political values, attitudes and knowledge, often through agents such as family, school and the media
citizens are stripped of their voting rights
a political party expels a disloyal member
questions.explanation: Political socialisation is the lifelong process, shaped by agents like family, schools, peer groups and the media, through which individuals develop their political beliefs and orientations.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Civil Service is best described as the body of
options: permanent, paid officials who implement government policies, remaining in post regardless of changes in the ruling party
military officers who administer government during coups
temporary staff hired only during election periods
elected politicians who form the government of the day
questions.explanation: The Civil Service consists of permanent, professional and politically neutral officials who carry out government policy and administration continuously, regardless of which party is in power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One key feature that distinguishes the Civil Service from the political executive is that civil servants are expected to be
options: appointed solely on the basis of political party loyalty
elected directly by the people every four years
free to publicly campaign for the ruling party
politically neutral and anonymous in carrying out their duties
questions.explanation: Civil servants are traditionally expected to serve any government of the day impartially, remain anonymous in policy credit/blame, and avoid open partisan political activity.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A public corporation, such as the Nigerian National Petroleum Company, is best described as
options: a privately owned company with no government involvement
an agency responsible solely for organising elections
a department fully integrated into and directly controlled day-to-day by a government ministry
a body established by government to provide a service or run an enterprise on behalf of the State, often with a degree of operational autonomy
questions.explanation: Public corporations are created by law to run specific services or commercial enterprises for the State, typically enjoying more operational autonomy than an ordinary government ministry department.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a common advantage of public corporations over civil service departments?
options: Automatic profitability regardless of management
Total exemption from the country's tax laws
Complete freedom from any form of government oversight
Greater flexibility and autonomy in day-to-day management decisions
questions.explanation: Public corporations are usually given more operational and managerial flexibility than a civil service department, allowing quicker decision-making in running their specific enterprise.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principle of 'anonymity' in the Civil Service means that
options: civil servants generally do not take public credit or blame for government policy, which rests with the political head
civil servants work exclusively behind closed doors with no public interaction
civil servants cannot be identified by name in any government record
the identities of civil servants are kept permanently secret from the public
questions.explanation: Anonymity means civil servants advise and implement policy without publicly claiming credit or being publicly blamed; political responsibility rests with the minister or elected head.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Decentralisation in public administration refers to the
options: transfer of administrative powers and decision-making from the central government to lower levels of government or agencies
concentration of all administrative power at the centre
abolition of local government councils
removal of the civil service from government control entirely
questions.explanation: Decentralisation involves devolving authority and responsibility away from the central government to regional, local, or specialised bodies to improve efficiency and responsiveness.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Local government, as the third tier of government in Nigeria, is primarily established to
options: conduct Nigeria's foreign policy independently
replace the need for a state government entirely
control the national currency and monetary policy
bring government closer to the grassroots and provide services suited to local needs
questions.explanation: Local government exists to decentralise administration, ensuring services and development efforts are tailored to and delivered closer to communities at the grassroots level.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Yoruba political system was generally organised around
options: a system without any traditional titleholders
rule by an assembly of women elders exclusively
a completely stateless, decentralised society with no identifiable rulers
a centralised monarchy headed by an Oba, assisted by a council of chiefs such as the Oyo Mesi
questions.explanation: Traditional Yoruba states, such as the Oyo Empire, were centralised, with an Oba (king) at the apex, checked and advised by councils of chiefs like the Oyo Mesi.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the pre-colonial Oyo Empire, the traditional council of kingmakers and chiefs that could check the powers of the Alaafin, including compelling him to commit suicide, was known as the
options: Aro Confederacy
Sokoto Caliphate Council
Oyo Mesi
Egbe Omo Oduduwa
questions.explanation: The Oyo Mesi was a powerful council of chiefs led by the Bashorun, which served as a check on the Alaafin's power and could, in extreme cases, order him to take his own life.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Traditional Igbo political organisation before colonial rule is generally best described as
options: administered directly by British colonial officers
governed exclusively through Islamic emirate structures
a largely decentralised, republican system without a central king, relying on councils of elders, age grades and title societies
a strongly centralised empire ruled by a single hereditary emperor
questions.explanation: Much of pre-colonial Igbo society was famously acephalous (without central kingship), with authority diffused among councils of elders, age grades, and title-holding societies rather than a single monarch.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani political system, especially after the 1804 Jihad, was mainly organised as
options: a centralised emirate system under the Sokoto Caliphate, headed by the Sultan of Sokoto
a confederation of independent city-states with no overarching authority
a system of government based purely on matrilineal succession
a completely stateless society with no formal rulers
questions.explanation: Following Usman dan Fodio's Jihad of 1804, the Hausa states were consolidated into a highly centralised Islamic emirate system under the Sokoto Caliphate.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Usman dan Fodio is most notable in Nigerian pre-colonial history for
options: signing the treaty that ceded Lagos to Britain in 1861
leading the 1804 Jihad that established the Sokoto Caliphate
founding the ancient city of Ile-Ife
leading the Aba Women's Riot of 1929
questions.explanation: Usman dan Fodio led the 1804 Islamic reform movement (Jihad) against the Hausa kings, culminating in the establishment of the Sokoto Caliphate, one of the largest states in 19th-century Africa.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Aro Confederacy in pre-colonial Igbo land derived much of its political and economic influence from
options: control of the Long Juju oracle and dominance of the regional slave trade network
direct alliance with British colonial administrators
control of the trans-Saharan trade routes
possessing the only standing army in the region
questions.explanation: The Aro people extended influence across much of south-eastern Nigeria through the religious authority of the Ibinukpabi (Long Juju) oracle and their extensive trading and slave-trade networks.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Benin Kingdom's traditional political system was headed by the
options: Sultan, ruling directly over all of southern Nigeria
Emir, supported by a council of Islamic scholars
Oba, supported by palace chiefs and town chiefs
elected President chosen by popular vote
questions.explanation: The historic Benin Kingdom was a centralised monarchy under an Oba, whose authority was exercised with the support of palace chiefs (Uzama) and town chiefs.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect Rule, as practised by the British in colonial Nigeria, was a system in which
options: traditional rulers were abolished immediately upon colonisation
Nigeria was granted full self-government from the outset of colonisation
the colonial government ruled through existing traditional rulers and institutions under British supervision
Britain administered the colony entirely through British-appointed officials with no role for traditional rulers
questions.explanation: Indirect Rule, notably associated with Lord Lugard, used existing traditional authorities as agents of colonial administration at the local level, under the ultimate supervision of British officials.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Lord Frederick Lugard is most closely associated with
options: the amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates of Nigeria in 1914
leading Nigeria to independence in 1960
drafting Nigeria's 1979 Constitution
founding the Sokoto Caliphate
questions.explanation: As Governor-General, Lord Lugard oversaw the 1914 amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates into a single colony known as Nigeria.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect Rule proved comparatively more difficult to implement effectively among the Igbo than among the Hausa-Fulani mainly because
options: the Igbo had no contact whatsoever with British colonial officials
the Hausa-Fulani rejected all forms of colonial administration
Igbo society was largely decentralised without the kind of established centralised chieftaincy that Indirect Rule assumed
the Igbo already had a written constitution before colonisation
questions.explanation: Because much of Igbo land lacked centralised kingship structures, the British often imposed artificial 'Warrant Chiefs', which proved a poor fit and contributed to unrest such as the Aba Women's Riot of 1929.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Aba Women's Riot of 1929 was primarily triggered by
options: the signing of the Treaty of Berlin in 1885
the outbreak of the Nigerian Civil War
the introduction of Indirect Rule in Northern Nigeria
fears that the colonial government intended to extend taxation to women, following the activities of Warrant Chiefs
questions.explanation: The riot arose from women's anger over the census exercise and Warrant Chief abuses, widely feared to be a precursor to taxing women, sparking mass protests across south-eastern Nigeria.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1914 amalgamation of Nigeria's Northern and Southern Protectorates was carried out mainly to
options: abolish the office of Governor-General
reduce the administrative costs of governing the two protectorates separately and allow the South to subsidise the North
create separate, permanently independent regions
immediately prepare Nigeria for full independence
questions.explanation: A major motivation for amalgamation was administrative and financial efficiency, as the more revenue-rich South could help subsidise the less commercially developed North under a single administration.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 is notable in Nigerian constitutional history mainly for
options: abolishing the Legislative Council entirely
granting Nigeria full independence
creating the three regions of North, East and West
introducing the elective principle, allowing Nigerians to elect a limited number of representatives to the Legislative Council for the first time
questions.explanation: The 1922 Clifford Constitution was historic for introducing limited elections, allowing Lagos and Calabar to elect a small number of members to the Legislative Council.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 is significant mainly because it
options: created the Mid-Western Region
abolished regional Houses of Assembly
granted Nigeria full independence from Britain
introduced a greater degree of Nigerian participation in central government through an expanded Council of Ministers
questions.explanation: The Macpherson Constitution expanded Nigerian representation and introduced a central Council of Ministers, giving Nigerians a larger, though still limited, role in central governance.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 is most notable for
options: granting Nigeria's independence
introducing the presidential system of government
formally establishing Nigeria as a federation of three regions plus the federal territory of Lagos
abolishing the regional premiers
questions.explanation: The 1954 Lyttleton Constitution formally entrenched federalism in Nigeria, establishing the Federation comprising the Northern, Western and Eastern Regions and the federal territory of Lagos.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria attained independence from British colonial rule on
options: 1 October 1963
15 January 1966
1 October 1960
questions.explanation: Nigeria became an independent country on 1 October 1960, though it remained a monarchy under the British Crown until it became a republic on 1 October 1963.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria became a republic, replacing the British monarch as Head of State with a Nigerian President, on
options: 1 October 1963
12 June 1993
1 October 1960
questions.explanation: On 1 October 1963, Nigeria adopted a Republican Constitution, replacing Queen Elizabeth II as Head of State with a Nigerian ceremonial President, while retaining a parliamentary system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under the 1963 Republican Constitution, who served as Nigeria's first indigenous, ceremonial President?
options: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa
Obafemi Awolowo
Yakubu Gowon
Nnamdi Azikiwe
questions.explanation: Nnamdi Azikiwe, who had earlier been Governor-General, became Nigeria's first President under the 1963 Republican Constitution, a largely ceremonial role in the parliamentary system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under Nigeria's First Republic (1963-1966), who served as Prime Minister and effective head of government?
options: Ahmadu Bello
Nnamdi Azikiwe
Aguiyi-Ironsi
Abubakar Tafawa Balewa
questions.explanation: Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa served as Nigeria's Prime Minister, the head of government under the parliamentary system of the First Republic, until the January 1966 coup.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1979 Constitution marked a significant shift in Nigeria's system of government by introducing
options: a return to the parliamentary system used in the First Republic
a purely military form of administration
a confederal arrangement among the regions
a presidential system of government, modelled largely on that of the United States
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution, which ushered in the Second Republic, abandoned the Westminster parliamentary model for a US-style presidential system with separation of powers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Who became Nigeria's first executive President under the 1979 Constitution?
options: Shehu Shagari
Muhammadu Buhari
Olusegun Obasanjo
Ibrahim Babangida
questions.explanation: Alhaji Shehu Shagari of the National Party of Nigeria (NPN) was elected and inaugurated as Nigeria's first executive President in October 1979, ushering in the Second Republic.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1999 Constitution, which currently governs Nigeria, came into effect on
options: 1 October 1979
1 October 1960
12 June 1993
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution took effect on 29 May 1999, the day military rule formally ended and Olusegun Obasanjo was inaugurated as President, marking the start of the Fourth Republic.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major criticism often levelled against the 1999 Constitution is that it
options: was the first Nigerian constitution to introduce federalism
was never actually implemented
was promulgated by a military government rather than being drafted through a fully representative constituent assembly
abolished the office of the President entirely
questions.explanation: Critics argue the 1999 Constitution lacked full legitimacy because it was largely handed down by the outgoing military government rather than emerging from broad popular deliberation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The June 12, 1993 presidential election, widely regarded as Nigeria's freest and fairest, was controversially annulled under the regime of
options: General Yakubu Gowon
General Muhammadu Buhari
General Ibrahim Babangida
General Sani Abacha
questions.explanation: The June 12, 1993 election, believed to have been won by Chief M.K.O. Abiola, was annulled by the military government of General Ibrahim Babangida, triggering a major political crisis.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's first military coup, which toppled the First Republic, took place on
options: 31 December 1983
29 July 1966
1 October 1960
15 January 1966
questions.explanation: The 15 January 1966 coup, led by a group of young army officers, overthrew the civilian government of the First Republic and led to the assassination of key political leaders, including Prime Minister Balewa.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Following the January 1966 coup, who emerged as Nigeria's first military Head of State?
options: General Sani Abacha
General Yakubu Gowon
Major General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi
General Murtala Mohammed
questions.explanation: Major General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi assumed power as Nigeria's first military Head of State after the January 1966 coup, before being killed in the July 1966 counter-coup.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The July 1966 counter-coup in Nigeria led to the emergence of which military ruler?
options: General Aguiyi-Ironsi
General Olusegun Obasanjo
General Muhammadu Buhari
General Yakubu Gowon
questions.explanation: The July 1966 counter-coup brought Lieutenant Colonel Yakubu Gowon to power as Head of State, and his tenure saw the outbreak and end of the Nigerian Civil War (1967-1970).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: General Murtala Mohammed, who became Head of State in 1975, was in office for a relatively short period mainly because he
options: lost a general election
resigned due to ill health
was assassinated in an attempted coup in February 1976
voluntarily handed over power to a civilian government within months
questions.explanation: General Murtala Mohammed was assassinated in the abortive coup led by Lieutenant Colonel Buka Suka Dimka on 13 February 1976, after less than a year in office.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which military Head of State handed over power to a democratically elected civilian government in 1979, ending the first period of military rule?
options: General Yakubu Gowon
General Olusegun Obasanjo
General Ibrahim Babangida
General Sani Abacha
questions.explanation: General Olusegun Obasanjo, who succeeded the assassinated Murtala Mohammed in 1976, oversaw the transition programme that returned Nigeria to civilian rule under the Second Republic in 1979.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The military coup that terminated Nigeria's Second Republic and ousted President Shehu Shagari occurred on
options: 31 December 1983
17 November 1993
15 January 1966
12 June 1993
questions.explanation: On 31 December 1983, a military coup led by Major General Muhammadu Buhari overthrew the civilian Shagari administration, ending the Second Republic.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: General Ibrahim Babangida is particularly notable in Nigerian political history for
options: being Nigeria's first military Head of State
handing over power peacefully to a civilian president in 1979
annulling the June 12, 1993 presidential election
leading Nigeria during the Civil War
questions.explanation: General Babangida's regime (1985-1993) is most remembered for the controversial annulment of the June 12, 1993 election, one of the most consequential events in Nigeria's political history.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Following the political crisis after the annulment of the June 12, 1993 election, an Interim National Government was headed by
options: General Abdulsalami Abubakar
Chief M.K.O. Abiola
Chief Ernest Shonekan
General Sani Abacha
questions.explanation: Chief Ernest Shonekan headed the short-lived Interim National Government (ING) from August to November 1993, before being pushed out in a palace coup by General Sani Abacha.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The military Head of State whose regime organised the transition programme that culminated in the return to civilian rule on 29 May 1999 was
options: General Muhammadu Buhari
General Ibrahim Babangida
General Abdulsalami Abubakar
General Sani Abacha
questions.explanation: General Abdulsalami Abubakar became Head of State after Abacha's death in June 1998 and swiftly organised the transition programme that led to the inauguration of the Fourth Republic on 29 May 1999.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The central, longstanding pillar of Nigeria's foreign policy, especially reflected in its diplomatic engagement across the continent, is often summarised as
options: strict non-alignment with any international body
Africa as the centrepiece of Nigeria's foreign policy
isolationism from all regional affairs
permanent military alliance with a single foreign power
questions.explanation: Since independence, successive Nigerian governments have consistently emphasised Africa, and particularly African liberation, unity and development, as the central focus of the country's foreign policy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's foreign policy of Afrocentrism was most visibly demonstrated through its
options: withdrawal from the United Nations
refusal to join any regional or international organisation
strong support for the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa and liberation movements across Southern Africa
alliance with apartheid South Africa's government
questions.explanation: Nigeria was a vocal and material supporter of anti-colonial and anti-apartheid liberation movements, including the African National Congress, reflecting its Africa-centred foreign policy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's leadership role in founding the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Monitoring Group, ECOMOG, was primarily aimed at
options: policing internal Nigerian elections
coordinating West African monetary union
providing a peacekeeping force to help resolve the civil conflicts in Liberia and Sierra Leone
creating a joint West African military alliance against a foreign colonial power
questions.explanation: ECOMOG, in which Nigeria played the leading role, was deployed as a regional peacekeeping force to help contain and resolve the devastating civil wars in Liberia and, later, Sierra Leone.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principle of 'non-alignment' in Nigeria's Cold War-era foreign policy meant that Nigeria
options: refused all forms of foreign trade
avoided formal military alliance with either the Western (NATO) bloc or the Eastern (Soviet) bloc
aligned exclusively with the United States and NATO
aligned exclusively with the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: As a non-aligned nation, Nigeria sought to avoid entangling itself in the Cold War rivalry between the Western and Eastern blocs, preferring to engage both sides on its own terms.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's foreign policy principle of respect for the 'sovereign equality of all African states' primarily means that Nigeria
options: considers itself formally superior in status to smaller African states
excludes smaller states from regional organisations
treats all African states, regardless of size or power, as equal and independent in international relations
seeks to annex smaller neighbouring states
questions.explanation: This principle reflects Nigeria's commitment to treating fellow African states as sovereign equals in diplomacy, despite differences in size, population or economic strength.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's diplomatic and economic pressure on the apartheid government of South Africa included
options: establishing full diplomatic relations with apartheid South Africa
withdrawing entirely from the Commonwealth in support of apartheid
providing military assistance to the apartheid government
nationalising British Petroleum's Nigerian assets in 1979 to protest Britain's ties with apartheid South Africa
questions.explanation: In 1979, Nigeria nationalised British Petroleum's local operations to protest Britain's continued economic dealings with the apartheid regime in South Africa, illustrating its firm anti-apartheid stance.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The United Nations Organisation was formally established in
questions.explanation: The United Nations was founded in 1945, after the Second World War, to promote international peace, security and cooperation, succeeding the earlier League of Nations.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principal organ of the United Nations charged with primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security is the
options: International Court of Justice
Security Council
Economic and Social Council
General Assembly
questions.explanation: Under the UN Charter, the Security Council bears primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security, including the power to authorise sanctions or the use of force.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The African Union (AU), which replaced the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) in 2002, was primarily established to
options: promote greater unity, solidarity and cooperation among African states
serve exclusively as a military alliance against non-African states
regulate global oil prices
replace all individual national governments in Africa
questions.explanation: The AU succeeded the OAU with an expanded mandate to deepen political and economic integration, promote peace and security, and foster unity and development across the African continent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was established in 1975 primarily to promote
options: a single political union merging all member states into one country
economic integration and cooperation among West African states
the abolition of all national currencies in West Africa
military conquest of non-member West African territories
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was created by the Treaty of Lagos in 1975 to foster economic cooperation, trade integration and collective development among its West African member states.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Commonwealth of Nations, of which Nigeria is a member, is best described as
options: a formal military alliance under British command
a voluntary association of mostly former British colonies that cooperate on shared democratic and developmental goals
a body with compulsory, legally binding authority over member states' domestic laws
an exclusively European economic union
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of independent states, most of them former British colonies, that work together on shared values such as democracy, development and human rights.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's membership of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) is primarily aimed at
options: managing global public health policy
regulating the price of agricultural exports
coordinating petroleum production policies with other oil-exporting countries to stabilise oil markets and prices
coordinating African peacekeeping missions
questions.explanation: As an OPEC member, Nigeria coordinates with fellow oil-producing nations on production quotas and pricing policy aimed at stabilising the international petroleum market.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the primary function of the International Court of Justice (ICJ)?
options: Prosecuting individual war criminals exclusively
Administering peacekeeping missions directly
Settling legal disputes between States and giving advisory opinions on international legal questions
Enforcing trade tariffs among member states
questions.explanation: The ICJ, the UN's principal judicial organ, settles legal disputes submitted by States and provides advisory opinions on international legal questions referred by authorised UN bodies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's dispute with Cameroon over the Bakassi Peninsula was ultimately resolved through
options: mediation solely by the African Union with no judicial involvement
a full-scale war between the two countries
unilateral annexation by Nigeria
a ruling of the International Court of Justice, followed by the Green Tree Agreement
questions.explanation: The ICJ ruled on the Bakassi Peninsula dispute in 2002, and Nigeria and Cameroon subsequently implemented the transfer of the territory through the 2006 Green Tree Agreement.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The primary purpose of the World Health Organization (WHO), a specialised agency of the UN, is to
options: direct and coordinate international public health efforts and set global health standards
provide peacekeeping troops for conflict zones
settle territorial disputes between member states
regulate international trade tariffs
questions.explanation: The WHO is the UN specialised agency responsible for coordinating global public health matters, including disease control, health standards and emergency health responses.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which international organisation is primarily responsible for promoting international monetary cooperation and providing financial assistance to member countries facing balance-of-payments problems?
options: The World Trade Organization
The International Labour Organization
UNESCO
The International Monetary Fund (IMF)
questions.explanation: The IMF works to foster global monetary cooperation, financial stability, and facilitates international trade, including offering financial assistance to countries experiencing balance-of-payments difficulties.
